Learn from outcomes · experimental model

Let your experience make the estimate.

Record an expectation before an event. Afterward, record its reward and how you feel. The app fits a personal version of the reward-and-expectations equation.

Everyday-life adaptation of Rutledge and colleagues’ 2014 model. The original evidence concerns reward tasks. This adaptation is experimental and predicts immediate reported feelings, not long-term happiness or the causal benefit of a choice.

1. Before it happens

Reward means how rewarding the event itself is: 0 = no reward, 10 = extremely rewarding. This is different from your overall happiness afterward. Use this meaning consistently.

2. After it happens

Your model’s evidence

Estimate the next event

Formula, fitting, and limits

H(t) = w₀ + w₁ Σ γ^(t−j) CRⱼ + w₂ Σ γ^(t−j) EVⱼ + w₃ Σ γ^(t−j) RPEⱼ. For certain events CR is the known reward and EV/RPE are zero. For uncertain events EV is your expected reward, RPE is actual reward minus expected reward, and CR is zero.

This app fits a ridge regression (penalty 1, unpenalized intercept). It selects γ from 0, .25, .5, .75, .9 using forward validation within the oldest 70% of observations. The newest 30% are held out to compare mean absolute error with a fixed training-mean baseline. Only afterward are coefficients refit on all observations for the next-event estimate. Prediction outputs are bounded to 0–10.

24 observations is a product minimum for a first check, not a scientific sufficiency threshold. At most the latest 200 matching-scale observations are used. Decay is per recorded event, not elapsed hours. Log promptly in event order. Events from different scale definitions are kept separate. Categories are pooled; context, sleep, personality, and many other factors are not modeled. A small error on this history does not establish future accuracy. Scenario endpoints are conditional outcomes, not probabilities or confidence intervals. No simulated records are added to your history.

Evidence and interpretation · November 2, 2026

Enjoy it now. Still value it later?

Research can suggest better questions. It cannot calculate which purchase or relationship will make you happiest.

Luxury clothing: pleasure, use, identity, and adaptation

A 2026 review of 109 articles describes several routes from luxury consumption to well-being, including enjoyment, identity, and meaning. It also calls for stronger longitudinal evidence. It does not supply a dependable happiness return for a designer item. Luxury consumption review.

Possessions are not automatically worse than experiences. In two studies measuring feelings over two weeks, material purchases provided more frequent moments of happiness; experiences provided more intense moments. One experiment used C$20 purchases, so this is not evidence about the long-term effect of an expensive jacket. Weidman & Dunn, 2016.

Our design interpretation: ask whether you would enjoy using it, whether you would still want it without an audience, and what you expect after the novelty fades. Cost per use is arithmetic based on your guess; it is not happiness per dollar.

Saving: future options and financial security

A study of 585 UK bank customers linked higher accessible balances with perceived financial well-being and life satisfaction, even with several other financial factors accounted for. It was observational: it does not prove that saving a specific amount causes a specific happiness gain. Ruberton, Gladstone & Lyubomirsky, 2016.

Our design interpretation: compare a purchase with the actual goal or security you would preserve by saving. Saving is not always the happier choice; enjoying an affordable purchase can matter too. The goal-delay calculation excludes investment returns.

Relationships: connection, uncertainty, and autonomy

Three studies connected psychological need fulfillment with relationship functioning and well-being. Feeling connected and being able to choose freely both matter. These findings concern relationship processes; they do not predict a stranger’s interest or your chance of rejection. Patrick and colleagues, 2007.

Our design interpretation: compare a bounded invitation, a smaller plan, and stepping back. Consider best and difficult outcomes, what you can comfortably give, and whether interest is mutual. Uncertainty is not rejection; rejection is not a measure of your worth. No amount spent obligates another person.

Energy: what can and cannot be calculated

NASA-TLX measures subjective workload across different demands; it is not a battery meter. Sleep quality matters as well as duration, and sleep needs vary by age. Neither source provides a formula converting sleep and meals into your daily usable mental or emotional energy. NASA-TLX · CDC sleep guidance.

The earlier energy-point formula was an invented planning convention. We removed it. This version calculates only your planned time balance and keeps effort and capacity as self-reports. Log what happened afterward to see which expectations fit your life.

Another factor that matters to you

Avoid counting the same benefit twice: free time already includes recovery; energy covers workload intensity. Only weight relationship, health, or security effects separately when they add something beyond those measures. Scores are your expectations.

Hard limits override the score. The optional 20%-raise time preference above remains a separate check; it is not counted twice in the combined score.

Score = 50 + 50 × weighted mean of factor changes. Income uses ln(B/A) divided by ln(1 + your major percentage change); time and effort use savings divided by your major change. Rating changes use (B − A)/10. Each factor is capped at −1 to +1. A score above 55 leans toward the higher-income option, below 45 toward the current option, and 45–55 is a close call. These are app conventions, not validated happiness thresholds.

Keep the effort rating about intensity, not duration. Recovery time should exclude work and commuting already entered. These are your estimates; sleep cannot determine an exact energy supply.

Calculation and assumptions

Income index change = 100 × ln(option B income / option A income). A doubling adds 69.3 index points at any starting income. This borrows the approximate log-income shape observed in the 2021 study; it does not use a fitted happiness coefficient. It is an income comparison index, not happiness points, a percentage happiness increase, or a causal prediction.

Time = work + commute + additional recovery. Effort load = work-and-commute hours × effort rating / 10, expressed in self-rated equivalent full-effort hours. This is a planning convention, not measured biological energy; recovery is shown separately.

If you supply a personal time limit for a 20% raise, the comparison uses your exchange rate: ln(1.2) / that limit. Preference margin = ln(B/A) − exchange rate × extra weekly time. The break-even income is A × exp(exchange rate × extra weekly time). This is a local preference model, assumes a constant exchange rate, and does not value effort separately or determine whether a job is right for you.

Income is before tax. Extra spending, benefits, job security, taxes, and changes in household needs are excluded. The research does not establish a universal plateau, so this calculation imposes none. Read the evidence and its limits ↓

Income & well-being · evidence reviewed November 2, 2026

How much money is enough for happiness?

The evidence: higher income generally goes with better well-being, with smaller gains per extra dollar. Whether those gains eventually flatten depends on the population, measurement, and analysis. The research supports a relationship, not a salary that guarantees happiness.

Two outcomes matter: emotional well-being is how you feel during daily life; life evaluation is how satisfied you are with your life overall. They can respond differently to income.

The major findings — and what the amounts mean

2010 · About $75,000 for daily feelings; no plateau for life evaluation. Kahneman and Deaton analyzed over 450,000 U.S. responses collected in 2008–2009. The figure refers to annual household income before tax, and is the midpoint of a $60,000–$90,000 income category. It was never a precise individual salary requirement. PNAS · original study.

2018 · Global estimates: $95,000 for life evaluation; $60,000–$75,000 for emotional well-being. Jebb and colleagues analyzed approximately 1.7 million observations across 164 countries. These are annual incomes adjusted for household size and purchasing power, expressed in international dollars, not ordinary individual salaries. Estimated life-evaluation satiation varied by region: Northern America was $105,000. The high-income end has fewer observations, which makes turning points less certain. Nature Human Behaviour · original study.

2021 · Real-time feelings continued improving beyond $75,000. Killingsworth used 1,725,994 real-time reports from 33,391 employed U.S. adults. Experienced well-being and life evaluation rose approximately with the logarithm of annual household income, without the earlier $75,000 plateau. This was a volunteer smartphone sample, not a representative sample of everyone. PNAS · original study.

2023 · Around $100,000 was a plateau for the least happy group, not the whole sample. Killingsworth, Kahneman, and Mellers jointly reanalyzed the 2021 data. Emotional well-being flattened near that income for roughly the least happy 15–20%; it kept rising among happier participants, and rose faster above that level for the happiest group. This reuses the same dataset rather than providing an independent replication. PNAS · joint reanalysis.

All dollar figures above are reported in their studies’ units. They have not been converted to 2026 dollars. Converting an old amount for inflation would update purchasing power, not establish a new happiness cutoff.

Newer evidence: what it adds, and what it cannot settle

2024 · Wealthy groups reported higher life satisfaction. An author-posted report by Killingsworth compared a U.S. income sample with two high-net-worth samples. The wealthy groups scored higher than respondents earning over $500,000 annually. However, wealth is not salary; the samples differ in country and collection period. This is evidence against a simple ceiling, not a recommended income target. Author’s research report.

2024 · Some analyses still find satiation. An Insee working paper using five surveys reports country-specific and sometimes partial plateaus. This helps explain why a single cutoff remains disputed: survey design and the fitted relationship affect the conclusion. Insee working paper.

2025 · Context matters. Another author-posted report using real-time feelings from 29,138 employed U.S. adults found higher personal income associated with greater happiness outside work, but no significant association while working. It does not show that a pay rise causes either pattern. Author’s research report.

These newer reports are identified separately from the peer-reviewed journal papers above; they do not all have the same publication status or study design.

Does more money actually cause greater well-being?

Most salary studies compare different people, so they cannot isolate what a raise would do for you. Stronger causal evidence comes from other settings: a Swedish lottery study found larger randomly assigned prizes produced lasting gains in life satisfaction, with smaller effects on happiness and mental health. That concerns a wealth windfall, not an annual salary threshold. Review of Economic Studies · lottery study.

A randomized study giving 200 people $10,000 found improvements in well-being compared with controls, with larger benefits in lower-income countries. This supports money having real benefits in that setting; a one-time transfer cannot identify an “enough per year” figure. PNAS · cash-transfer experiment.

How to use this in your decisions

Think in percentage gains and what money makes possible. In a log-income relationship, equal percentage increases correspond to similar average well-being differences. For example, $50,000 → $60,000 and $100,000 → $120,000 are both 20% increases. That does not predict the same happiness change for two individuals.

Your annual goal in the decision form is a personal planning input. Set it around your household’s costs, financial buffer, goals, and the working hours needed to earn it. Compare the benefit of extra income with the time, stress, and opportunities it costs. Income alone cannot produce a defensible personal 0–10 happiness score.

Spending also matters: a 2017 field experiment found working adults reported greater happiness after a time-saving purchase than after a material purchase. Consider whether an affordable purchase would actually free time you value, and record what happens afterward. PNAS · buying time study.
